items.title: Narrative review of acupuncture for tinnitus again finds evidence too weak and inconsistent to confirm efficacy
items.whyMatters: A new review of acupuncture for tinnitus concludes what earlier systematic reviews already found: the studies are small, inconsistent and hard to blind, so there is still no reliable proof it helps. It offers ideas about how acupuncture might act on the brain and inner ear, but no new patient data.
items.summary: Nothing substantively new: a narrative review that re-summarizes tinnitus pathophysiology, mainstream Western interventions, and proposed acupuncture mechanisms, and concludes — consistent with existing systematic reviews already in the database — that acupuncture trials are heterogeneous, small, single-center and lack high-quality evidence of stable efficacy.

detail.population: Not reported — narrative review of published literature, no defined patient sample
detail.primaryEndpoint: Not reported — no prespecified endpoint; narrative synthesis of mechanisms and clinical literature
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — the review makes only vague claims that acupuncture can 'alleviate tinnitus symptoms to a certain extent' and reports no psychoacoustic loudness matching or loudness rating data.
detail.distressOutcome: none — no pooled or quantitative distress (THI/TFI/TQ) outcomes are presented, and the authors state unified high-quality evidence is lacking.
detail.otherOutcomes: Mentions autonomic regulation and quality-of-life impact narratively; no quantitative sleep, QoL or hearing outcomes reported.
detail.safety: Not reported — no adverse event data (e.g. needling complications) presented in the abstract/record.
limitations: Narrative review, not a systematic review or meta-analysis; no risk-of-bias assessment or pooled effect estimates
No quantitative data, no effect sizes, no distinction between loudness and distress outcomes
Underlying acupuncture literature acknowledged by the authors as heterogeneous (acupoints, manipulation), single-center, small-sample, with inconsistent outcome measures
Placebo/expectancy effects cannot be isolated in the cited trials; blinding of needling is inherently difficult
Long-term (>1 year) follow-up data scarce
Mechanistic claims (cochlear microcirculation, GABA upregulation, default-mode-network remodeling) rest largely on animal/imaging studies that cannot establish clinical benefit
Published in a general-medicine journal outside the tinnitus/audiology literature; likely regional publication bias toward acupuncture literature
detail.funding: independent — authors (PLA General Hospital, Beijing) declare no conflicts of interest; no funding disclosed in the record. Note potential non-financial orientation toward traditional Chinese medicine, though the abstract is explicitly self-critical.
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Tinnitus Functional Index questionnaire translated and validated for European Portuguese
items.whyMatters: The TFI is a standard questionnaire for measuring how much tinnitus bothers you and whether treatment helps; this study makes a Portuguese version available so Portuguese patients can be assessed with the same yardstick used internationally. It does not test any treatment and does not change what is known about what works.
items.summary: A European Portuguese translation and cultural adaptation of the Tinnitus Functional Index, validated in a small single-centre sample (n=30) showing high internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha 0.96) and strong correlation with the THI (rho = 0.823). Cronbach's alpha = 0.96; Spearman rho with THI = 0.823, p < 0.001; N = 30, mean age 57 ± 11.5 years

detail.population: Adults with tinnitus attending a Portuguese tertiary hospital ENT department, aged 26-80 (mean 57 ± 11.5 years), 19 of 30 female
detail.primaryEndpoint: Psychometric properties of the European Portuguese TFI: internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha) and convergent validity against the THI (Spearman rho)
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Formal translation/back-translation and expert-panel cultural adaptation process; not reported: test-retest reliability, factor structure, responsiveness to change, or minimal clinically important difference
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — this is a questionnaire validation study; the TFI measures tinnitus impact/distress and says nothing about the loudness of the percept itself.
detail.distressOutcome: none — no treatment was given and no distress change was measured; the study only shows the translated instrument measures distress consistently.
detail.safety: Not reported — questionnaire validation study with no intervention.
limitations: Very small sample (n=30) for a psychometric validation
Single tertiary centre, likely more severe/selected patients; limited generalizability
No test-retest reliability reported
No confirmatory factor analysis of the eight TFI subscales
Responsiveness to treatment change not tested, despite the stated aim of using it in intervention studies
No minimal clinically important difference established for this version
Cross-sectional design; convergent validity assessed against only one comparator (THI)
Full text in Portuguese; only abstract-level detail available for review
detail.funding: unclear — no funding or conflict-of-interest statement available in the record; all authors are hospital/university ENT clinicians with no apparent commercial ties, so independent academic work is likely.
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Small placebo-controlled trial of a single dose of nicotine gum for tinnitus loudness completes; results not yet posted
items.whyMatters: Researchers ran a small, properly blinded test of whether one piece of 4 mg nicotine gum briefly changes how loud tinnitus actually sounds — measured by sound-matching rather than by questionnaires. The trial has finished but no results are public yet, so there is no reason to expect benefit, and nicotine carries its own risks including dependence.
items.summary: A registry status update: a small investigator-initiated crossover trial at San Diego State University testing whether a single 4 mg dose of nicotine polacrilex gum acutely changes psychoacoustic tinnitus loudness in non-smoking adults is now marked COMPLETED (primary completion 2026-08-03, n=29). No results have been posted, so the finding — positive or negative — is still unknown; the novelty is the mechanism (nicotinic acetylcholine receptor modulation) being tested in humans for tinnitus with loudness matching as the primary endpoint.

detail.population: Non-smoking adults aged 18-80 (fewer than 100 lifetime cigarettes, none in past year, FTND ≤2, negative urinary cotinine) with chronic subjective tinnitus of at least 6 months' duration
detail.primaryEndpoint: Within-session change (post minus pre) in psychoacoustic tinnitus loudness match (dB sensation level, method of adjustment at the tinnitus pitch), nicotine session vs placebo session
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Auditory selective attention (Coordinate Response Measure percent correct) after administration, nicotine vs placebo; pre-specified baseline-only measures included THI, TFI and pure-tone audiometry (0.25-12 kHz)
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — the trial is designed around the correct endpoint (psychoacoustic loudness matching, not questionnaires), but no outcome data have been posted, so nothing can yet be said about the tinnitus percept.
detail.distressOutcome: none — THI and TFI were collected at baseline only, as descriptive characterization; this design cannot measure change in tinnitus distress.
detail.otherOutcomes: Baseline audiometry (0.25-12 kHz) collected for characterization only; no post-treatment hearing, sleep, or quality-of-life outcomes.
detail.safety: Not reported — no adverse event data in the registry record; the record notes no data monitoring committee, and nicotine exposure in nicotine-naive adults raises predictable nausea/dizziness/cardiovascular and dependence considerations that will need explicit reporting.
limitations: No results posted — completion status only; efficacy direction entirely unknown
Very small sample (n=29) at a single site
Single acute dose with outcomes up to 2 hours; says nothing about durable benefit
Loudness matching is variable within and across sessions; a 2-period crossover with no repeated baselines is vulnerable to measurement noise and regression effects
Blinding of an active drug with perceptible subjective effects (nicotine in naive users) is hard to maintain despite flavor-matched placebo and blindfolding; no blinding-integrity outcome listed
No distress/functional change outcomes (THI/TFI baseline only)
No safety or tolerability outcome measure pre-specified in the record
Nicotine is a widely used substance with prior mixed/anecdotal reports of worsening tinnitus; net risk-benefit unaddressed
detail.funding: independent — lead sponsor San Diego State University with an internal SEED grant; no manufacturer sponsorship listed. Commercial products (Nicorette, Trident) were used as intervention and placebo without stated industry involvement.
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: FDA clears next-generation Levo tinnitus device through the 510(k) substantial-equivalence pathway
items.whyMatters: FDA 510(k) clearance means a device may legally be sold because it is similar enough to a device already on the market — it is not a ruling that the device reduces tinnitus. The clinical evidence for the Levo sleep-time sound approach remains limited and unchanged by this decision.
items.summary: An FDA 510(k) database record indicating that a next-generation device, the Levo Gen 2 Tinnitus Therapy System (Levo Medical Corporation), received a Substantially Equivalent decision (K260413) on 2026-09-04. This is a marketing-clearance administrative milestone for an already-marketed device family, not new clinical data.

detail.population: Not reported (510(k) decisions rest on substantial equivalence to a predicate device, not necessarily on new clinical testing in patients)
detail.primaryEndpoint: Not reported — 510(k) review determines substantial equivalence to a legally marketed predicate, not efficacy against a clinical endpoint
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — a 510(k) clearance record contains no psychoacoustic loudness matching or percept-loudness data whatsoever, so it says nothing about the tinnitus sound itself.
detail.distressOutcome: none — no THI/TFI/TQ or any distress outcome is reported in a substantial-equivalence decision record.
detail.safety: Not reported — the metadata contains no adverse-event data; substantial equivalence implies FDA found no new questions of safety or effectiveness relative to the predicate, but no study-level safety numbers are available here.
limitations: Regulatory administrative record, not clinical evidence — no patients, no endpoints, no comparator
510(k) clearance is explicitly NOT an FDA finding of efficacy and is not 'approval' or 'De Novo authorization'
Primary record could not be retrieved by a fetcher; device name, applicant, indications-for-use wording and predicate device are unverified beyond the metadata line
Applicant listed as 'Levo Medical Corporation' — the original Levo System was marketed by Otoharmonics; the corporate relationship/name change is unconfirmed
No information on whether any clinical data at all were submitted in support of the Gen 2 device
detail.funding: independent (record is generated by FDA, not by the sponsor), but the underlying submission is by the device manufacturer and any accompanying claims about Gen 2 performance should be treated as manufacturer-originated until a paper or trial registry entry exists
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Survey of 428 adults with tinnitus finds anxiety, depression and pain are the quality-of-life areas most affected
items.whyMatters: In this group, the parts of daily life most affected by tinnitus were emotional health and pain rather than mobility or self-care, and a smaller subgroup carried a much heavier burden across anxiety, depression and sleep. It supports assessing and treating those comorbidities alongside tinnitus, but it does not test or endorse any specific treatment.
items.summary: A cross-sectional secondary analysis of pooled baseline data (N=428) from internet-CBT tinnitus trials profiling health-related quality of life using EQ-5D-5L dimensions, showing pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression are the most affected domains and identifying a small high-burden cluster with greater psychological and sleep distress despite no demographic or audiological differences. No problems reported: mobility 76.6%, self-care 92.5%, usual activities 65.2%; affected: pain/discomfort 33.4%, anxiety/depression 40.2%. A 10-point TFI increase associated with 53% higher odds of worse usual activities and 51% higher odds of worse anxiety/depression. Fully healthy EQ-5D-5L profile vs any problem: mean TFI 39.0 vs 55.3 (d = 0.78).

detail.population: Adults with tinnitus enrolled at baseline in several internet-based CBT efficacy trials (mean age 54.9 years, 51.9% female); recruitment channels and countries not detailed in the abstract
detail.primaryEndpoint: EQ-5D-5L profile dimensions (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression) and their association with tinnitus severity (TFI)
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Cluster-analysis-derived HRQoL profiles; associations with psychological and sleep-related distress measures and audiological/demographic variables
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — this is a descriptive HRQoL profiling study with no psychoacoustic loudness matching or loudness rating of the percept; nothing here says anything about the tinnitus sound itself.
detail.distressOutcome: none — it is a cross-sectional baseline association study, not a treatment evaluation, so it demonstrates that higher tinnitus severity co-occurs with worse emotional and functional HRQoL but provides no evidence that any intervention reduces distress.
detail.otherOutcomes: Quality of life is the core outcome: anxiety/depression and pain/discomfort dimensions most affected; sleep disturbance characterized the high-burden cluster. No hearing or audiological differentiators found between profiles.
limitations: Cross-sectional baseline analysis — no causal inference and no treatment outcome data
Sample is drawn from people who volunteered for internet-CBT trials, so it is self-selected, internet-capable, and likely more distressed and less representative than the general tinnitus population
Pooled data from several trials with potentially differing eligibility criteria and measurement contexts
EQ-5D-5L is a generic, coarse five-level measure that is not tinnitus-specific and may miss tinnitus-relevant burden
Cluster analysis is exploratory and data-dependent; profiles require independent replication
Associations are correlational — comorbid anxiety, depression, pain, and insomnia may drive or be driven by tinnitus severity
No loudness or psychoacoustic measurement of any kind
detail.funding: unclear — funding and COI statements are not visible in the abstract record. Authors include prominent internet-CBT for tinnitus investigators (Beukes, Andersson, Manchaiah) whose own trial data supplied this sample; Andersson and Beukes have authored ICBT programs, so an intellectual/program interest should be assumed pending the full disclosure statement. No manufacturer funding evident.
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Danish nationwide registry: 5.7% of childhood cancer patients have recorded hearing loss or tinnitus as a late effect
items.whyMatters: This study counts how often children treated for cancer later show up in national health records with hearing loss or tinnitus, and finds the risk is highest in the youngest children and those given high-dose chemotherapy. It supports routine hearing monitoring for childhood cancer survivors, but it tests no tinnitus treatment and changes nothing about which therapies work.
items.summary: A Danish nationwide registry study (2014–2024) quantifies auditory late effects — hearing loss and tinnitus combined — in 3075 children diagnosed with cancer before age 18, reporting a 5.7% prevalence with higher risk in younger children, malignant neoplasms, and high-dose chemotherapy. It is new descriptive national epidemiology of ototoxicity, not evidence about any tinnitus treatment. Prevalence of auditory late effects 5.7% of 3075 children; higher risk among younger patients, patients with malignant neoplasms, and those receiving high-dose chemotherapy at a younger age (relative risks and chi-square tests reported in full text; no separate tinnitus-only prevalence given in the abstract)

detail.population: Children and adolescents in Denmark diagnosed with cancer before age 18 between 2014 and 2024, identified via the Danish Cancer Register and Danish National Patient Register
detail.primaryEndpoint: Prevalence of registry-coded auditory late effects (hearing loss and/or tinnitus) among childhood cancer patients
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Associations of auditory late effects with age at diagnosis, cancer type (malignant vs other), and high-dose chemotherapy exposure; temporal trend analysis
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — no psychoacoustic loudness matching or percept rating was performed; this is a registry prevalence study with no treatment and no tinnitus loudness measurement.
detail.distressOutcome: none — no THI/TFI/TQ or other validated distress instrument was administered; quality-of-life implications are asserted in the discussion, not measured.
detail.otherOutcomes: Hearing loss is bundled with tinnitus into a single 'auditory late effects' outcome; no separate hearing thresholds, sleep, or validated QoL data reported in the abstract
detail.safety: Not reported as a safety study; the finding that high-dose chemotherapy in younger children is associated with higher auditory late-effect risk is consistent with well-established platinum/aminoglycoside ototoxicity rather than a new signal.
limitations: Tinnitus is not reported separately from hearing loss — the 5.7% figure is a combined 'auditory late effects' outcome, so tinnitus prevalence cannot be extracted
Registry/ICD-code ascertainment almost certainly underestimates tinnitus, which is subjective and often uncoded, especially in young children
No non-cancer comparison cohort, so excess risk versus the general paediatric population cannot be estimated
No audiometric or psychoacoustic verification; no severity, loudness, or distress grading
Cross-sectional prevalence with variable and possibly short follow-up (diagnoses through 2024) — delayed-onset ototoxicity may be missed
Only the abstract is available (online ahead of print); effect sizes, confidence intervals, and COI statement not verifiable from the record supplied
detail.funding: unclear — no funding or conflict-of-interest statement is present in the supplied record; authors are hospital-based clinicians (Rigshospitalet ENT/Audiology and Paediatric Oncology), with no manufacturer involvement apparent
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Korean national survey: bothersome tinnitus linked to more depression and stress during COVID-19 restrictions
items.whyMatters: In a large national health survey, people whose tinnitus bothered them a lot reported more depressive symptoms and stress during the 2020 lockdown period, but not in 2022 — suggesting that outside stressors and reduced access to care can hit the most bothered tinnitus patients hardest. It says nothing about whether any treatment works, and nothing about how loud tinnitus is.
items.summary: A weighted national survey analysis (KNHANES 2020 vs 2022) showing that people with bothersome chronic tinnitus had higher depressive symptoms and stress specifically during the COVID-19 restriction period, with those differences disappearing in the 2022 'living-with-COVID' period. It is new only as epidemiological context on how external stressors interact with tinnitus severity; it tests no treatment. During the restriction period, the bothersome tinnitus group had significantly higher PHQ-9 scores and higher prevalence of depressive symptoms and high stress vs non-tinnitus (p < 0.001 for all) and vs non-bothersome tinnitus (p < 0.05 for all); no significant group differences in 2022; within the bothersome tinnitus group, 2020 vs 2022 differed for PHQ-9 (p = 0.048), depressive symptoms (p = 0.009) and high stress (p = 0.039). No effect sizes, prevalence percentages or confidence intervals reported in the abstract.

detail.population: Korean adults from the 8th (2020) and 9th (2022) Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, classified as bothersome tinnitus (VAS > 4), non-bothersome tinnitus (VAS ≤ 4), or no tinnitus
detail.primaryEndpoint: Depressive symptoms by PHQ-9 (cut-off ≥5) and self-reported high stress, compared across tinnitus groups and between the 2020 restriction period and the 2022 living-with-COVID period
detail.secondaryEndpoints: PHQ-9 continuous scores; group comparisons between bothersome and non-bothersome tinnitus
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — no psychoacoustic loudness matching or loudness rating was performed; tinnitus was captured only as a bothersomeness VAS, which is a distress/annoyance measure, not loudness.
detail.distressOutcome: none — this is an observational association between tinnitus bothersomeness and depression/stress, not a treatment effect on distress; it describes burden rather than any improvement.
detail.otherOutcomes: Not reported (no sleep, QoL, or audiometric outcomes described in the abstract)
detail.safety: Not reported (observational survey analysis; no intervention administered)
limitations: Cross-sectional survey data from two separate years — not a longitudinal cohort, so no individual-level change can be established
Tinnitus defined by a single-item bothersomeness VAS rather than validated instruments (THI/TFI) or audiometric confirmation
Self-reported depression (PHQ-9) and stress; no clinical diagnosis
Ecological/confounded attribution to the pandemic — other 2020-vs-2022 differences (survey participation, healthcare access, economic conditions) could explain the pattern
No effect sizes, prevalence figures or confidence intervals in the abstract; only p-values
Korean national sample; generalizability to other health systems uncertain
The 'need for non-face-to-face management' conclusion is an inference, not tested by the data
detail.funding: independent — funded by clinical research grants from Seoul National University Boramae Medical Center (02-2025-0041) and Hanyang University research fund (HY-202500000003190); competing interests declared as none; no manufacturer involvement.
detail.source: European archives of oto-rhino-laryngology : official journal of the European Federation of Oto-Rhino-Laryngological Societies (EUFOS) : affiliated with the German Society for Oto-Rhino-Laryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Large US survey analysis: tinnitus and depression partly explain the link between noise exposure and poor sleep
items.whyMatters: In 8,539 US adults, both noise exposure and tinnitus were associated with trouble sleeping, and tinnitus plus depression statistically accounted for part of the noise-sleep link. This is observational survey data that reinforces why sleep and mood are treated alongside tinnitus, but it tests no treatment and changes nothing about what works.
items.summary: A cross-sectional NHANES (2006-2020, n=8539) analysis estimating that tinnitus and depression statistically mediate 12.76%-37.80% of the association between environmental/occupational noise exposure and trouble sleeping, with the counterintuitive finding that speech-frequency hearing loss appeared 'protective' against trouble sleeping. It adds pathway-level (mediation) modelling to the already well-known tinnitus-sleep association, but nothing about treatment. Workplace noise adjusted OR = 1.145 (95% CI 1.015-1.292, P = 0.027); off-work noise adjusted OR = 1.165 (1.005-1.348, P = 0.042); tinnitus adjusted OR = 1.648 (1.442-1.882, P < 0.001); speech-frequency hearing loss adjusted OR = 0.767 (0.660-0.891, P = 0.001); tinnitus and depression mediated 12.76%-37.80% of total effects; hearing thresholds ≥20 dB linked to reduced risk of trouble sleeping (inverted U-shaped trends in some subgroups)

detail.population: US adults in NHANES 2006-2020 cycles with audiometry, noise-exposure and sleep questionnaire data
detail.primaryEndpoint: Self-reported trouble sleeping (NHANES sleep questionnaire item), modelled against workplace and off-work noise exposure
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Mediation by tinnitus, speech-frequency hearing loss and mental illness (depression); subgroup and restricted cubic spline analyses of hearing thresholds
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — no psychoacoustic or perceptual loudness measurement of any kind was performed; tinnitus was a self-reported yes/no exposure variable.
detail.distressOutcome: none — no validated tinnitus distress instrument (THI/TFI/TQ) and no intervention; the tinnitus-sleep odds ratio is an observational association, not a distress outcome.
detail.otherOutcomes: Sleep: tinnitus and noise exposure both independently associated with self-reported trouble sleeping; hearing: speech-frequency hearing loss associated with LOWER odds of trouble sleeping (biologically implausible as protection, plausibly reduced perception of nocturnal noise or residual confounding/selection); mental health: depression acted as a partial mediator.
limitations: Cross-sectional design — mediation analysis implies temporal ordering that the data cannot establish; reverse causation (poor sleep amplifying tinnitus) is equally compatible
Self-reported tinnitus, noise exposure and sleep trouble; no validated tinnitus severity measure (THI/TFI) and no objective sleep measurement (no polysomnography or actigraphy)
'Protective' effect of speech-frequency hearing loss is biologically implausible and suggests residual confounding, collider bias or misclassification rather than a real protective mechanism
Pooling many NHANES cycles with differing audiometry/questionnaire availability introduces selection effects; no correction detail for multiple subgroup and spline analyses in the abstract
No treatment, no randomization, no control condition — cannot inform any therapy rating
Funding and conflict-of-interest statements not visible in the available record
detail.funding: unclear — no funding or COI statement in the available record; authors are hospital-based ENT clinicians in Chengdu, China, with no apparent manufacturer involvement
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.
